2. Use only the tools offered in the request, with their argument names and allowed values.
3. Cite evidence by the exact id attributes in the context (for example "ev-3f9a2c-007").

5. Answer only in the required format.

Failure mechanisms (choose the one the evidence supports, for the service that must be fixed):
- bad_deployment: a recent release of that service introduced its errors. The errors start
  shortly after the deploy and are the service's own (its logs show the failing code).
  Put the bad release in "version".
- resource_pressure: the service runs out of memory or CPU: OOMKilled events, memory close to
  its limit, restarts.
- dependency_failure: the service fails only because a service it calls is failing. Put that
  service in "dependency"; the fix belongs to the dependency, so investigate it next.
- unknown: none of these is supported by the evidence yet.
When failures pass through several services (A calls B, B calls C), claim each link the
evidence supports (a dependency_failure on A with dependency B, on B with dependency C), and
claim the deepest service's own failure (for example resource_pressure on C) as soon as its
own evidence shows it: RECAP fixes the deepest supported cause.

<untrusted_data id="runbook-memory-pressure#overview-1" kind="doc" flags="" source="doc:fixtures/knowledge/runbook-memory-pressure.md#Overview">
[Runbook: memory pressure and crash loops > Overview]
Memory pressure means a container is using nearly all of its memory limit. When it
crosses the limit it is killed and restarted, and if the leak continues the pod ends up
in a crash loop.
</untrusted_data>
<untrusted_data id="runbook-k8s-crash-loops-and-rollouts#diagnosis-crash-loop-or-image-pull-1" kind="doc" flags="" source="doc:fixtures/knowledge-overlays/kubernetes/runbook-k8s-crash-loops-and-rollouts.md#Diagnosis: crash loop or image pull">
[Runbook: Kubernetes rollouts that stall and pods that crash loop > Diagnosis: crash loop or image pull]
1. Call `get_k8s_like_events` for the service. `CrashLoopBackOff` means the code starts and
   exits; `BackOff` after an `OOMKilled` termination means memory (see the readiness and
   memory runbook); `ImagePullBackOff` means the image itself.
2. For a crash loop, read `get_service_logs`: the last lines before each exit name the
   error. An exception tagged with a release, such as `[build <release>]` or
   `(version=<release>)`, points at the code of that release.
3. For an image-pull back-off the logs are empty. Compare the newest revision with the one
   before it in `get_recent_deployments`.
4. Compare times with `get_recent_deployments` and the `error_rate` metric. A crash loop
   that begins within minutes of the service's own release makes that release a suspect. A
   crash loop on a service that was not released points elsewhere: memory, configuration, or
   a dependency it needs at start-up.
</untrusted_data>
<untrusted_data id="runbook-k8s-crash-loops-and-rollouts#symptoms-1" kind="doc" flags="" source="doc:fixtures/knowledge-overlays/kubernetes/runbook-k8s-crash-loops-and-rollouts.md#Symptoms">
[Runbook: Kubernetes rollouts that stall and pods that crash loop > Symptoms]
- `CrashLoopBackOff`: a container starts, exits, and the kubelet waits longer before each
  restart. The restarts metric climbs and ready replicas stay below desired.
- `ImagePullBackOff` or `ErrImagePull`: the node cannot pull the image. The pod is stuck
  before its container starts, so it writes no logs at all.
- A rollout that is stuck: fewer updated replicas than desired and, once the progress
  deadline has passed, the Deployment condition `ProgressDeadlineExceeded`.
- Errors that begin when the rollout begins, on the service being rolled out.
</untrusted_data>
<untrusted_data id="runbook-memory-pressure#symptoms-1" kind="doc" flags="" source="doc:fixtures/knowledge/runbook-memory-pressure.md#Symptoms">
[Runbook: memory pressure and crash loops > Symptoms]
- `OOMKilled` events: a container exceeded its memory limit and was killed.
- `BackOff` events and a `CrashLoopBackOff` status while the pod keeps restarting.
- Readiness probe failures, so fewer replicas are ready than desired.
- The memory metric climbs toward the limit; logs show heap warnings and
  `OutOfMemoryError` lines.
- The error rate rises because the remaining replicas take all the traffic.
</untrusted_data>
